blocks.value: **Inheritance enables the use of an existing class to define a new class.**

items: A **derived class** is defined by adding instance variables and methods to an existing class. Also known as **subclass**, **child class**, or **descendant class**.
The existing class the derived class is built upon is the **base class**. Also called **superclass**, **parent class**, or **ancestor class**.

blocks.value: The derived class is `Student`; the base class is `Person`. **`Student` inherits the declared instance variables and public methods of `Person`, except its constructors.**

`Student` never declares `name`, yet every `Student` has one. Note also that `Student` must call `getName()` rather than using `name` directly, `name` is `private` in `Person`, and **private members are not accessible even to subclasses**. (`protected` would allow it, at the cost of some encapsulation.)

A class that does not say `extends` still has a parent: Java makes it extend the built-in class `Object`. That is the top of every inheritance chain, which is why every object already has methods such as `toString()` and `equals()`, even in a class that never wrote them:
